questions.q: What distinction from T-SQL carries over directly to Snowflake?
options: Functions return computed values usable inline in a SELECT and can't run DML; stored procedures can run DML/DDL and are invoked separately
Snowflake merges functions and stored procedures into a single object type
Only stored procedures exist in Snowflake, not functions
Functions in Snowflake can run UPDATE and DELETE statements directly
questions.explain: The functional split between UDFs (computed values, no side effects) and stored procedures (procedural logic, DML/DDL allowed) is unchanged from T-SQL — only the syntax for writing each differs.

questions.q: How do you invoke a stored procedure in Snowflake?
questions.explain: Snowflake uses CALL to invoke stored procedures — T-SQL's EXEC has no place in Snowflake syntax.

questions.q: What is the assignment operator used inside a Snowflake Scripting procedure body?
questions.explain: Snowflake Scripting uses := for assignment inside a procedure body, rather than T-SQL's SET variable = value pattern.

questions.q: What characterizes a SQL UDF compared to a stored procedure?
options: It is a single expression with no procedural block or side effects, returning a computed value usable inline in a query
It can run UPDATE and DELETE statements just like a stored procedure
It must be invoked with CALL, exactly like a stored procedure
It requires a DECLARE and BEGIN/END block
questions.explain: A SQL UDF is just an expression (no BEGIN/END, no DML) — the same restriction T-SQL scalar functions have when used inline in a SELECT.

questions.q: Besides SQL, what other languages does Snowflake support for writing UDFs?
options: Only SQL is supported — no other languages
Snowflake UDFs cannot use any programming language, only expressions
questions.explain: Snowflake supports UDFs written in JavaScript and Python (and others), useful when logic is awkward to express in pure SQL — called the same way as SQL UDFs once created.
